docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This page serves as an evidence portfolio of the work completed throughout the semester in the Embedded Systems course, taught by Professor Oliver Ochoa Garcia.

docs.title: Course Objective
docs.text:
Learn to design and program embedded systems at the hardware level using the RP2350, integrating sensors, actuators, communication, and real-time processing to develop autonomous and functional systems.

Within this course, fundamental topics for the development and programming of embedded systems are covered, including:

  • Development Environment Setup — Installation and use of the Pico SDK, CMake, GDB, and OpenOCD, as well as ESD safety practices.
  • Low-Level Programming — Register-level programming, GPIO, bitwise operations, finite state machines (FSMs), timers, and interrupts.
  • Serial Communication — Implementation of UART, ring buffers, command-line interfaces (CLI), and debugging techniques.
  • Sensor and Actuator Interfacing — Use of PWM to control LEDs, servomotors, and DC motors, as well as ADC for analog signal acquisition and processing.
  • Signal Processing and Generation — Implementation of PIO (Programmable I/O) and DMA to efficiently generate, capture, and transfer signals.
  • Performance and Reliability — Analysis of performance, latency, and jitter; use of watchdogs, low-power techniques, EMC, memory architecture, and multicore programming.
  • Testing and Validation — Application of unit testing and debugging techniques to verify proper system operation.
  • Capstone Project: Micromouse — Integration of the acquired knowledge to develop an autonomous system capable of navigating a competitive environment.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text: Goal: to understand and control GPIO peripherals through memory-mapped registers, bitwise operations, masks, and RP2350 SIO registers.

docs.title: What I Learned
docs.text: In this practice, I learned how to control the GPIO pins of the RP2W and how each register affects their behavior. I also learned how binary numbers and masks can be used to control specific pins, and how the << operation moves bits to create the value needed. Finally, I understood better how the Pico SDK functions work and how they are connected to the SIO registers.

docs.title: Exercise 1 — 4 bit binary counter
docs.text:
Use the four LEDs as a 4-bit binary number.

The program must count: 1 → 2 → 3 → ... → 15 → 0

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:

The code worked, but it was quite different from what our teacher later explained in class. After going over the concepts again, especially binary numbers and masks, we were able to write our own code.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
For this exercise, we used what we had learned about binary masks to control more than one LED at the same time. We first turned on the two LEDs on the outside using 1001, and then the two LEDs in the middle using 0110. After that, we turned them off in the same order.

docs.title: What could have gone better
docs.text: Even though all of our codes worked correctly, I think we could have paid more attention to the theory from the beginning. We also could have experimented more with the circuit and the program to better understand how everything works. This would have helped us feel more confident with the code instead of mainly focusing on getting the expected result.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Overall, this practice helped us understand better how the GPIO pins and LEDs can be controlled using binary values and masks. At first, we were a little confused about the theory, but after reviewing it and practicing with different codes, we were able to create the four animations successfully. It also helped us see how small changes in the code can create different patterns and made us more comfortable working with the RP2350.

docs.title: Digital inputs
docs.text: Goal: Learn how to configure and use digital inputs on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 understanding pull-ups, pull-downs and debounce techniques to correctly read buttons and avoid unstable signals.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: In this practice, I learned how to configure and use digital inputs on the Raspberry Pi Pico 2 to read the state of a button. I also learned how pull-up and pull-down resistors prevent inputs from floating and how the input can be read as a high or low logic level. Finally, I understood the importance of debounce and how it helps avoid false readings caused by the mechanical bouncing of a button.

For this exercise, we used what we had learned about digital inputs to control four LEDs using a switch. We programmed the LEDs to turn on only when exactly one of the two buttons was pressed, using a logical XOR condition. The LEDs stayed off when neither button or both buttons were pressed, helping us understand how XOR works with multiple digital inputs.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
For this exercise, we used a switch to control a counter from 0 to 3 and four LEDs to show the current position of the counter. One button increased the counter and the other decreased it, while a flag made sure each press was counted only once instead of repeating while the button was held. The counter also wrapped around at both ends of the four-LED bus.

Code: 

while (true) {
    // With an external pull-up, pressed = 0 (low level)
    if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u << PIN_BA)) && (flag == 0)) {
        counter++;
        flag = 1;
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    else if (!(sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u << PIN_BB)) && (flag == 0)) {
        counter--;
        flag = 1;
        sio_hw->gpio_clr = MASK;
    }
    else if ((sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u << PIN_BA)) &&
             (sio_hw->gpio_in & (1u << PIN_BB))) {
        flag = 0;
    }
    if (counter > 3) {
        counter = 0;
    }
    else if (counter < 0) {
        counter = 3;
    }
    sio_hw->gpio_set = (1u << (counter + 10));
    sleep_ms(100);
}

docs.text: Even though all of our codes worked correctly, I think we could have experimented more with the circuit and the program to better understand how everything works. This would have helped us feel more confident with the code instead of mainly focusing on getting the expected result.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Overall, this practice helped us understand better how digital inputs work and how buttons can be used to control the GPIO pins of the Raspberry Pi Pico 2. At first, we were a little confused about pull-ups, pull-downs, and debounce, but after reviewing the theory and testing the code, we were able to read the button states correctly. It also helped us understand the importance of avoiding floating inputs and made us more comfortable working with digital inputs and the RP2350.

docs.title: What We did
docs.text:
For the exam, we created a game based on Lights Out, using a breadboard with a 3×3 matrix of 9 LEDs and 10 buttons. One of the buttons was used to generate a random initial configuration of the LEDs, while the other nine buttons corresponded to each LED in the matrix.

The objective of the game was to turn off all 9 LEDs by using the buttons. Every time one of the buttons was pressed, the state of the corresponding LEDs changed, so the player had to find the correct combination of buttons to turn them all off.

When the player successfully turned off all the LEDs, the program detected the winning condition and showed a victory signal by making all the LEDs flash. This allowed us to test the operation of the buttons as inputs and the LEDs as outputs, while also working with programming sequences and the logic needed to detect the winning condition.

const uint32_t botones = (1u << B1) | (1u << B2) | (1u << B3) | (1u << B4) | (1u << B5) | (1u << B6) | (1u << B7) | (1u << B8) | (1u << B9) | (1u << BR);

static const uint32_t enemigosmortales[9] = {   // lo que va a prender
    (1u << L1) | (1u << L2) | (1u << L4), (1u << L2) | (1u << L1) | (1u << L3) | (1u << L5),
    (1u << L3) | (1u << L2) | (1u << L6), (1u << L4) | (1u << L1) | (1u << L5) | (1u << L7),
    (1u << L5) | (1u << L2) | (1u << L4) | (1u << L6) | (1u << L8), (1u << L6) | (1u << L3) | (1u << L5) | (1u << L9),
    (1u << L7) | (1u << L4) | (1u << L8), (1u << L8) | (1u << L5) | (1u << L7) | (1u << L9),
    (1u << L9) | (1u << L6) | (1u << L8)
};
volatile uint32_t pendientes = 0; // Guarda  botones que fueron presionados
static uint32_t rng_estado;
static void rng_semilla(void) {
    rng_estado = (uint32_t)time_us_64();
    if (rng_estado == 0) rng_estado = 0xA5A5A5A5; // no puede arrancar en 0
}
static uint32_t mi_rand32(void) { //num. aleatorio
    uint32_t x = rng_estado;
    x ^= x << 13;
    x ^= x >> 17;
    x ^= x << 5;
    rng_estado = x;
    return x;
}
static void generar_tablero(void) // patrón aleatorio de LEDs prendidos
{
    uint32_t patron;
    do {
        patron = mi_rand32() & leds;
    }
    while (patron == 0);
    sio_hw->gpio_clr = leds;  // apaga todos los leds
    sio_hw->gpio_set = patron;  // enciende los leds del patrón
}
static void isr_botones(uint pin, uint32_t event_mask)
{
    gpio_acknowledge_irq(pin, event_mask);  // confirma que la interrupción fue atendida
    if (event_mask & GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL) // comprueba si ocurrió un flanco de bajada
    {
        pendientes |= (1u << pin); // guarda botón fue presionado
    }
}
int main(void)
        {//principal
    gpio_init_mask(leds | botones);   // inicia los GPIO
    sio_hw->gpio_oe_set = leds;  
    sio_hw->gpio_oe_clr = botones;
    gpio_pull_up(B1); // Activa el pull-up de cada botón
    gpio_pull_up(B2);
    gpio_pull_up(B3);
    gpio_pull_up(B4);
    gpio_pull_up(B5);
    gpio_pull_up(B6);
    gpio_pull_up(B7);
    gpio_pull_up(B8);
    gpio_pull_up(B9);
    gpio_pull_up(BR); //boton reinicio

    gpio_set_irq_enabled_with_callback(BR, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL,true, &isr_botones); // registra la función de int. para el botón de reinicio.
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B1, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);   // activa la int. de cada botón
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B2, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B3, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B4, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B5, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B6, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B7, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B8, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);
    gpio_set_irq_enabled(B9, GPIO_IRQ_EDGE_FALL, true);

    irq_set_priority(IO_IRQ_BANK0, 0xC0); // configura prioridad
    irq_set_enabled(IO_IRQ_BANK0, true);  // da la interrupción GPIO
    rng_semilla(); // inicia el generador aleatorio
    generar_tablero();   // Genera el primer tablero
    while (true) //bucle
    {
        if (pendientes)     // comprobamos si hay botón pendiente
        {
            sleep_ms(antir_ms);
            irq_set_enabled(IO_IRQ_BANK0, false);  // Desactiva int.
            uint32_t eventos = pendientes;  // Guarda los  pendientes
            pendientes = 0;   // Limpia los pendientes
            irq_set_enabled(IO_IRQ_BANK0, true); // Vuelve a activar int.
            uint32_t presionados =
                eventos & ~sio_hw->gpio_in;  // Lee botones presionados
            if (presionados & (1u << B1)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[0];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B2)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[1];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B3)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[2];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B4)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[3];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B5)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[4];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B6)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[5];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B7)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[6];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B8)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[7];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << B9)) {
                sio_hw->gpio_togl = enemigosmortales[8];
            }
            if (presionados & (1u << BR)){
                generar_tablero();
            }
             else if ((presionados & ~(1u << BR)) &&    // leds parpadean al mismo tiempo
                     (sio_hw->gpio_out & leds) == 0) {
                for (int i = 0; i < yupiyey ; i++) {
                    sio_hw->gpio_set = leds;
                    sleep_ms(vel);
                    sio_hw->gpio_clr = leds;
                    sleep_ms(vel);  //nueva partida

docs.title: Interrupts
docs.text: Goal: to understand how interrupts work on the RP2350, including IRQs, ISRs, GPIO interrupts, priorities, and how they allow the microcontroller to respond to events without constantly checking the inputs.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text: In this practice, I learned how interrupts allow the RP2350 to respond to events without continuously checking the GPIO inputs. I also learned how ISRs, IRQs, and the NVIC work together to handle interrupts, and how GPIO interrupts can be triggered by rising or falling edges. Finally, I understood how to configure GPIO interrupts using the Pico SDK and why it is important to acknowledge the interrupt and keep the ISR as short as possible.

docs.title: What could have gone better
docs.text: At first, the buttons for increasing and decreasing the speed were not working as expected. After testing and changing different parts of the code, I realized that I needed to remove the speed value controlled by the vel variable that we had previously declared as volatile. Once I made this change, the buttons worked correctly and I was able to control the speed as intended.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Overall, this practice helped us understand better how interrupts can be used to control different actions without constantly checking the buttons. At first, we had some problems getting the speed buttons to work, but after testing the code, we found the issue and were able to fix it. Creating the LED roulette also helped us understand how multiple interrupts and variables can work together to control the sequence, speed, and special action of the LEDs.

docs.title: PWM - Pulse Width Modulation
docs.text: Goal: to understand and implement Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) on the RP2350, control signal frequency and duty cycle, configure PWM slices and channels, and analyze how TOP and clock dividers affect signal resolution and output behavior.

docs.title: What I Learned
docs.text: In this practice, I learned how to use PWM to generate different sound frequencies and create musical notes using the RP2350. I also learned how changing the frequency and duty cycle affects the output signal and how PWM can be configured through the Pico SDK. Finally, I understood how a buzzer can be controlled to reproduce different tones, allowing us to build a simple electronic piano.

        }

        int selected_note = -1;
        for (uint i = 0; i < 10; ++i) {
            if (!gpio_get(note_buttons[i])) {
                selected_note = (int)i;
                break; // Si se mantienen varias teclas, tiene prioridad la de GPIO más bajo.
            }
        }

        if (selected_note >= 0) {
            float divider = (float)f_clk / (note_hz[selected_note] * (TOP + 1));
            uint16_t level = (uint16_t)(((TOP + 1) / 2) * volume / 100);
            pwm_set_chan_level(slice, chan, 0);
            pwm_set_clkdiv(slice, divider);
            pwm_set_chan_level(slice, chan, level);
        } else {
            pwm_set_chan_level(slice, chan, 0);
        }

        sleep_ms(5);
    }
}

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: this practice helped us understand how PWM works and how it can be used to generate different sound frequencies to create musical notes. By developing our electronic piano, we learned how to configure PWM using the Pico SDK and how frequency and duty cycle affect the output signal. Although programming the piano and finding the correct frequencies was challenging and took us longer than expected, we were able to apply the concepts we learned and understand how PWM can be used in practical applications. docs.title: Timers
docs.text: Goal: to understand and implement timer-based events in the RP2350, analyze timing characteristics, configure hardware alarms and interrupts, and use absolute deadlines to achieve precise and reliable periodic events.

docs.title: What I Learned
docs.text: In this practice, I learned how to use repeating timers in the RP2350 and how to measure their behavior using an oscilloscope. I also learned how period, frequency, duty cycle, latency, jitter, and drift affect a waveform. Finally, I understood how hardware alarms and interrupts work, how to configure them using registers, and why cumulative deadlines help maintain accurate periodic events.

docs.title: Part A - Predict first, measure second
docs.text:
In this activity, we programmed the RP2350 to toggle GPIO pin GP15 every 250 ms using a repeating timer from the Pico SDK. Before running the program, we calculated the expected timing characteristics of the signal, including the HIGH and LOW times, period, frequency, and duty cycle. Then, we used an oscilloscope to observe and measure the actual waveform, comparing the results with our theoretical calculations. As evidence, we recorded our measurements in a comparison table and captured videos of the oscilloscope displaying the generated signal.

Quantity Predicted Measured Difference Toggle interval 250 ms 249.8 ms 0.2 ms HIGH time 250 ms 249.8 ms 0.2 ms LOW time 250 ms 249.8 ms 0.2 ms Period 500 ms 499.8 ms 0.2 ms Frequency 2 Hz 2 Hz - Duty cycle 50% 50% -

docs.title: Part B -  Change only one variable
docs.text:
In this activity, we changed the TOGGLE_MS value to 100 ms, 50 ms, and 10 ms while keeping the rest of the program unchanged. Before each test, we calculated the expected frequency and waveform period, then used the oscilloscope to measure and compare the results. This allowed us to observe how changing the timer interval affects the signal frequency, HIGH and LOW times, and how the duty cycle remains approximately 50%. We also compared the usefulness of an LED and an oscilloscope when observing faster signals.

  1. Does TOGGLE_MS represent the waveform period? a. No, it represents the time between every status update
  2. What mathematical relationship connects TOGGLE_MS and the measured signal frequency? a. T = 2 × TOGGLE_MS and f = T/1
  3. Does changing TOGGLE_MS change the duty cycle? Why? a. No, it's still 50% because the time in Low and High is the same.
  4. At what point does observing the signal with an LED become less useful than observing it with an oscilloscope? a. When the signal changes too fast for us to notice the LED blinking.

docs.title: Part C -  Can the callback duration change the timing?
docs.text:
In this activity, we modified the repeating timer callback to measure how much time it spends executing. We used two GPIO pins: GP15 to display the timed output and GP14 to mark the beginning and end of the callback, allowing us to observe its execution time through the oscilloscope. We performed four experiments by changing the callback workload and switching between negative and positive timer delays. By comparing the waveforms on both channels, we observed how callback execution time affects the intervals between events and understood the importance of keeping callbacks and interrupts short.

  1. What does the width of the CH2 pulse represent? a. It represents the time that takes to execute the callback.
  2. What changes when the repeating-timer delay changes from negative to positive? a. With negative (-100 ms), the next callback is scheduled based on the start of the callback. With positive (+100 ms), the 100 ms start counting after the callback ends.
  3. Why should callbacks and ISRs normally be short? a. Because while they run, they use the CPU and can delay other tasks or events.
  4. What do you expect if the callback takes longer than the requested interval? a. The callback can take almost all the available time and events might get delayed or not run exactly at the requested interval.
  5. Does a longer callback necessarily change the HIGH/LOW duty cycle of CH1? Explain from the measured edges rather than from the source code alone. a. Not necessarily, you have to check it on the oscilloscope. If the HIGH and LOW changes still have roughly the same duration, the duty cycle will stay around 50%. The important thing is to measure the edges of CH1, not just assume it from the code.

docs.title: Part D — Make main() visibly do something else
docs.text: In this activity, we kept the repeating timer running on GP15 while using the main() function to perform an independent task, such as detecting push button presses. We made sure that the timer callback did not handle the button, allowing both tasks to run independently. Using the oscilloscope, we verified that interacting with the button did not significantly affect the timing of the output waveform. This helped us understand how hardware timers keep track of time independently of the main program, allowing the CPU to perform other tasks without interrupting periodic events.

docs.title: What could have gone better
docs.text: Although all the experiments worked correctly, we could improve our work by performing more measurements to obtain more accurate results and comparing them with the theoretical values. We could also test different timer intervals and callback workloads to better understand the limits of the RP2350 timer. Additionally, we could improve our documentation by explaining the small variations observed in the oscilloscope and analyzing how latency and jitter affect signal accuracy.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This practice helped us understand how timers work in the RP2350 and how they can generate periodic events without stopping the main program. Through the different experiments, we learned how to configure repeating timers, measure waveforms using an oscilloscope, and analyze characteristics such as period, frequency, duty cycle, latency, and jitter. We also explored how callback execution time and timer delays affect the generated signals, as well as how hardware alarms and interrupts work. Overall, we gained a better understanding of how hardware and software work together to manage time efficiently, allowing the microcontroller to perform multiple tasks while maintaining accurate timing.
